What are the true facts in regard to radioactive fall-out in connection with the Nevada bomb tests?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The facts in regard to radioactive fall-out as a result of the Nevada bomb tests were given in a report released by the United States atomic energy commission on February 15, 1955. These effects are described in paragraph 31 of the report which reads as follows:
"31. Only relatively small nuclear test explosions are conducted at the Nevada test site, in contrast to the tests of high yield thermonuclear devices at the Pacific proving grounds. In Nevada, as well as in the Pacific, all tests are planned for times when forecast weather conditions minimize the possibility of fall-out hazard. Methods of forecasting weather patterns in these areas are improving steadily. High air bursts at the Nevada testing grounds have produced no significant fallout and heavy fall-out from near surface explosions has extended only a few miles from the point of burst. The hazard has been successfully confined to the controlled area of the test site. The highest actual dose of radiation at an off-site community has been estimated to be less than one-third of the greatest amount of radiation which atomic energy workers are permitted to receive each year under the atomic energy commission's conservative safety standards."

1.	How many man hours were expended in shooting and preparing the documentary production entitled "Parliament at Work''?
2.	What is the estimated cost of the production, including a proportionate share of the annual salaries of the officials for the time engaged in its production?

1 and 2. The preparation of a documentary production on "Parliament at Work" was begun on February 15, 1955. Four hundred and seventy-nine man hours were expended on this project at an estimated cost, which includes everything used in computing government costs, of $3,430.65. Material photographed will not be scrapped but will be kept in the stock library for whatever use can be made of it in future.
3.	The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration first became aware that this film was being prepared about mid-day of March 10, 1955.

The film board officials in charge of the project themselves came to the conclusion that the material they had available would not make a satisfactory picture and that the project should be suspended and the material kept available in case it was decided, at a later date, to make a film on parliament at work. The minister concurred in this decision.

In

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: On a point of order then, Mr. Speaker, I understood Your Honour to rule a few minutes ago that when the hon. member was paraphrasing the article which he has in his hands he was taking the responsibility for the accuracy of the facts related in the article. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let us agree on this point. The hon. member is taking the responsibility for whatever he says. He could be paraphrasing a newspaper story without informing us that he is doing so. He is speaking as a member in this house and whatever he says he is responsible for. Now, it is precisely the objection which was raised by the minister the other day in which I supported him, that he could not be allowed to quote directly from the newspaper because other hon. members would perhaps quote directly from newspapers contradicting what the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace has been quoting. Therefore, instead of having an argument as between hon. members, we would have an argument as between newspapers and would have no facilities, as far as we are concerned, of ascertaining the accuracy of the stories [Mr. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace).)
which appeared therein. If the hon. member is making a statement and refers to some information which he has found somewhere he can espouse the information in his own words and make it his own. I mean, an hon. member may make a charge which is not necessarily well founded. But if he wants to make it upon his general responsibility as a member of this house I think we ought to let him do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: With all due deference to Your Honour, may I point out, sir, that the hon. member is not being argumentative. He is relating facts, and I believe that you just said, sir, that in doing so, he is taking the responsibility for what he is relating. He just refused to take that responsibility.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether we could not get it cleared up as to whether the hon. member is really infringing upon any rule of this house. Citation 265 of Beauchesne's third edition reads:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
I wonder whether the newspaper articles which the hon. member is attempting to read or to paraphrase come under the ban of that citation. If Your Honour will look in the concluding paragraph of the immediately preceding citation you will find that it reads:
Bourinot, page 335, refers to these objections when he says a member may read extracts from documents, books, or other printed publications as part of his speech, provided in so doing he does not infringe upon any point of order.
In the light of that, I wonder whether Your Honour could indicate what other points of order or ruling there might be that the hon. member is infringing upon. It seems to me that he is not out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the point was raised yesterday I was careful not to quote the two citations that the hon. member has referred to because they are not the two citations on which I anchored my decision. I look at the rule which says that a member must not read his speech. He must advance in support of it whatever he has to say, his own arguments, and not those of others, and no one will question that. What he was attempting to do was to support his views by what he said appeared in a newspaper. He went on to say that if a newspaper reporter should find certain things and report them in the detailed fashion that he has, he felt that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration could have done likewise. At that moment the minister rose and said: In another newspaper

someone else has contradicted the story referred to by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace. It was at that moment that I rose and said: Let us have the hon. member's own words and his own facts. If he wants to refer to information appearing elsewhere he may paraphrase it and take the responsibility for it. Let us not have an argument as between newspapers but as between members.
If the hon. member says: Here is a situation that exists. My own knowledge of this matter is very frail but I have here a newspaper story; that is my bible as far as the situation is concerned. An hon. member on the other side says: I have another newspaper and as far as I am concerned, this is the story. Where do we stand? Then we come to the question of the two citations to which the hon. member has referred. We have long citations from newspaper reports contradicting each other and not very much by way of what the hon. member himself should be saying when he addresses this house, namely, his own arguments, his own views and his own facts, facts within his own knowledge.
The reason I told the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources that it was difficult for me to go beyond what I have already said was this. Citation 262 of Beau-chesne's third edition says:
The practice of reading extracts from newspapers to support an argument in debate has been followed in the British house since 1840, when Speaker Peel, with the acquiescence of the house, allowed a member to proceed to read passages from a newspaper. In 1856, when a member was called to order for reading an extract from a newspaper, the Speaker stated that on former occasions when he had attempted to enforce this rule, he had been overruled by the house. A similar statement was made by the chairman in committee on March 9, 1857.
Now, I take this as an indication-and we know from our own experience here-that it has always been rather difficult to have this rule observed whereby an hon. member will not quote from newspapers in support of his own argument or whatever information he wants to supply to the house. If I am to err I would rather in this instance err on the side of generosity. I think that situation is one which the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace understands, and perhaps we might let him proceed a little further to find out if later on he will be exactly in order. If we find that he is going beyond what the rules allow, we can intervene again. At this moment I will let him go on.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Many of us on all sides of the house would be in difficulties if

I come now to the part played by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in this affair. It has already been indicated that undesirable aliens have been operating in the bookmaking business in Canada for something over two years and that for several months indications of such activities have been a matter of record through the press. I may say further that the names of many of these men are known-I am going to put some of them on the record in a few minutes-and are a matter of record in certain police forces in Canada. It is equally clear that the department has the power to inquire into and order the deportation of undesirable aliens who have entered Canada. Yet what has the department done? Nothing.
I want to know, for example, what the minister has done regarding the statement in the Toronto Telegram of February 22 which I paraphrased a little while ago, a statement that refers specifically to these people entering Canada by other means than through official immigration channels. These statements are not idle chatter. They are statements made by responsible newspapermen after considerable effort on their part which I, before coming here, have sincerely attempted to verify, and to the best of my knowledge and belief I have verified that these conditions exist. To give some idea of the type of men we are dealing with, let me tell you something about one of the men who has been operating in Montreal. He is Carmine Galenti, alias Galento, alias John Lelo, the name by which he is most commonly known in Montreal, alias John Surro. He is American born and has been in and around Montreal for most of the last three years and has been known, perhaps rightly, perhaps wrongly, as part owner of a certain restaurant which forms one of the hang-outs for the entire gang of thugs.
He was tried for murder, convicted of manslaughter in the second degree and sentenced to five to ten years. Subsequently he was paroled and later was picked up and served the rest of his sentence. He was convicted of felonious assault on a police officer, sentenced to 12i years and apparently

served it all. There are other charges against him in the United States. There are others, many of them, who have been engaged in this operation. The information is available, and I tell the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) that it is available no farther away from him than the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) through the Royal Canadian Mounted Police if he would only ask him for it, on at least 25 of these individuals, a number of whom may be easily identified as Americans with extremely questionable backgrounds and checkered careers both in Canada and the United States.
I have given the house the record of Galenti. Another who is well known is Camille Salim Joseph, alias Jacobs, who was actually convicted recently of keeping a bookmaking establishment. Then there are Michael Joseph Consolo, better known as Big Mike, Gilbert Beckley, Leo Schaeffer, Gino Campo, Jack Keithley and D. Geiger-man. These are names which are on record with the police department, and apparently the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has done nothing about them. If one is sincere, and I am sincere, one does not get these names and satisfy oneself sufficiently to be able to stand up and make such charges in the house without a tremendous amount of personal effort and a genuine attempt to establish the facts to one's satisfaction.
I wart the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to stand up and tell us why he has not looked into this situation because I do not think he can tell us he did not have some of this information over a period of a great many months. I want to know what relationship exists between one of these men and one with a very similar name who was investigated most thoroughly by the Kefauver inquiry in the United States. There is yet another with the same name and initials as a man who was identified during the Kefauver inquiry as the brother-in-law of Frank Costello, perhaps the most notorious witness before that inquiry and commonly accepted as one of the two top men in the United States underworld and racketeering organization.
For two years at least this group of people has been operating in and around Montreal. Particularly in later months the Montreal police department has done outstanding work in hampering their activities. May I say here that the remarks I am making are not a criticism in any way, shape or form of the Montreal police department. It is not the local police departments or the local municipal authorities who are at fault, and I think

the mayor of Outremont will agree with me in that statement. It is not the fault of the local organizations that these racketeers have chosen to move into their centres and concentrate their activities there. The police departments of the area are outstanding and they are doing everything they can to break up the group and drive these men away. But it is not part of their job to pick up and prosecute undesirable aliens and drive them out of Canada.
The sort of thing these American racketeers and gangsters are doing in Canada is like a cancer. Once it is established it spreads, grows and extends its tentacles all over the country. A little while ago these men were firmly established in Montreal. Perhaps knowing that my investigation was being carried on, and certainly as a result of the work of the Montreal police department, they seem to have been temporarily driven underground. But we can be sure, I think, that they will come up again. I think they will come up in Canada, Mr. Speaker, because of conditions previously outlined, unless we drive them right out of this country. I referred previously to Mr. Banks, and I just emphasize that as one indication again of the attitude that this citizenship and immigration department is prepared to take on occasion towards people who have known criminal records.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to sum up very briefly. First, organized crime, and that I think of as crime based on bookmaking and betting, is a serious danger to any community in which it exists. Secondly, such organized crime has been operating in and around Montreal for a number of years. Third, most of the key people in this operation have been United States gangsters, thugs and racketeers. Fourth, this has been a matter of general knowledge throughout most of the period, and police records exist with the R.C.M.P. and local police on most, if not all, of these men. Fifth, it has been possible for working newspapermen to establish these facts and make them a matter of public record. Sixth, despite all this the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has remained quiescent and has not taken steps to rid Canada of these undesirable aliens. Seventh, there has been no indication to this house some six weeks afterwards, nor any report, that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has taken official steps to remedy the situation or even investigate the charges made on February 22, both in the newspapers and in this house.

When I said that the R.C.M.P. were investigating reports similar to these, I meant precisely what I said.
The latest information I have is that that police investigation is still continuing. I do not think any reasonable person would expect a minister of citizenship and immigration to get up and give a progress report while a police investigation into some alleged crime was still going on. I can assure the hon. gentleman that as soon as the police or the hon. gentleman or anybody else puts in our hands information upon which we can take action in the courts with any reasonable chance of success, or on which we can deport any undesirable person who is here contrary to the law, there will be no time lost in doing that.

Since this question of quoting newspapers is one that often arises in debate, and about which certain points of order are quite often raised, I have looked into Beau-chesne's third edition further, and I find that on page 123, citation 303 refers to the responsibility a member must accept if he is quoting from a newspaper and basing his arguments on those quotations. The reference is to a question which is being asked on the orders of the day, as to whether or not the statement appearing in the press is true.
I am referring more particularly to the second paragraph of citation 303, and it seems to me there is a certain analogy there. The paragraph reads:
It is not in order to ask merely whether certain statements made in a newspaper are true; but attention may be drawn to such statements, if the member who puts the question makes himself responsible for their accuracy.
There is a certain analogy there between the principle advanced in this citation having to do with questions being asked of ministers and the situation with which we were confronted a moment ago. Whenever we base ourselves on a report in the newspaper or even paraphrase a document, I do not think one can avoid taking full responsibility as a member of this house for whatever one says.

Mr. Speaker, I will only take a few minutes of the valuable time of the house to voice a grievance. The house is already aware of the fact that on the occasion of the bicentenary of the deportation of the Acadians, a number of commemorative ceremonies will be held in various centres of the maritimes, of the province of Quebec and also in Louisiana where, as a matter of fact, some celebrations have already been held.
These observances, which have been organized in Canada as well as in the United States as a tribute to the survival and rebirth of the Acadian people, are of interest to over a million Canadians and Americans of Acadian descent.
They are also of interest to Englishspeaking Canadians from the maritimes, particularly those from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, who are generously co-operating in the organization of these celebrations.
There is an hon. member of the other place, for instance, a resident of Halifax, who has been enthusiastically taking part in this organizational work. Most of the maritime members of this house, in fact,

English as well as French-speaking, have extended to the organizers their kindest support. We know too that the state of Louisiana has already contributed a substantial amount to the fund set up by our Acadian cousins of that part of the United States for the purpose of these celebrations.
Next summer hundreds, even thousands, of visitors from Louisiana will come to this country, particularly to the maritimes. The conseil de la vie frangaise, under the skilled leadership of its secretary, Father Paul-Emile Gosselin, has already organized a useful tour of Louisiana by Canadians. It is also preparing several other friendship tours to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
This year, then, a continuous flow of tourists will bear down upon the maritime provinces. These friendship tours, these pilgrimages made by Canadians from central Canada to the maritimes, and particularly to Nova Scotia, will no doubt continue from year to year. In that province, formerly called Acadia, there are several historical sites particularly dear to the hearts of Canadians and Americans of Acadian descent.
This constitutes for Nova Scotia a source of income that is hardly tapped and that the Canadian government should help to develop, if only from a strict touristic point of view.
We just learned, through the provincial treasurer, Hon. Mr. Fielding, that the government of Nova Scotia has just decided to grant a generous subscription to the fund for the organization of the Acadian celebrations which will be held this year in that province.
Moreover, the government of Nova Scotia, through its information office, just issued a fine stamp, with inscriptions in both official languages, to commemorate the bicentenary of the deportation of the Acadians. Both decisions, bespeaking broad-mindedness and generosity, are well calculated to promote national unity in this country and certainly deserve to be called to the attention of this house. On behalf of the electors of Bonaventure county, whom I have the honour to represent in this house, about thirty thousand of whom are of Acadian origin, I wish to express deep gratitude to the premier of Nova Scotia and to his government for what they just did for the descendants of the first French pioneers who settled on the banks of the bays of Fundy and Chignecto.

Mr. Speaker, I rise very briefly to bring a grievance to the attention of the house, and I do so after a special request from many of my constituents who will not be able to hear the Easter programs on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation network. I am sorry the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) is not in his seat, but I am somewhat comforted by the fact that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) is listening to what I have to say.
As usual.

I know the Minister of Fisheries takes a very motherly interest in all things that occur in the interior of British Columbia.
The fact I wish to bring to the attention of the house is that there are still thousands of my constituents who are unable to hear Canadian stations or Canadian programs, or to listen to the C.B.C., while at the same time


millions of dollars are being spent on television in other parts of Canada. And we support that expenditure, of course.
For years chambers of commerce, farmers' institutes, labour organizations, the Canadian Legion and other organizations have passed resolutions asking that something be done to remedy this situation. As recently as last December a meeting was held in the Arrow lakes area which was attended by over 300 people from the Arrow-Slocan lakes. That meeting dealt with this question and passed a resolution urging the government to do something about improving radio reception at points where no programs, with the exception of those from the United States, are received.
During the last year low power relay transmitters have been established at Castle-gar and at Kaslo and I wish to say they are very much appreciated by the people in those districts. The very fact that these people are now able to receive C.B.C. programs from early morning until late in the evening has stimulated interest in these stations and strengthened the demand that something be done to serve the rest of the area. I have been told by officials of the C.B.C. that this can be done and I cannot understand why something has not been done to date.
It may be said to be a question of population but I do not think that that argument can hold because I know that low power relay transmitters have been established at points where the population is under 300 people, whereas these various organizations suggest that a transmitter at Nakusp would serve from 2,000 to 3,000 people; the station at Rosebery would serve some 2,000 to 3,000 people and the station at Balfour would serve from 3,000 to 4,000 people. So I contend that as far as population is concerned we should qualify for some attention in this regard.
I am told that it is also a matter of funds, but I would direct the attention of the minister and the officials to the fact that we are spending large sums of money to provide television service to the great majority of Canadians and I think it only right that pioneering people in the outlying districts should have a chance to listen to Canadian radio programs.
In that connection I have this year's report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in which low power relay stations are dealt with on page 52 as follows:
These are satellite transmitters of low power which are attached to the wire line networks at repeater points. These stations are able to relay programs only and are not able to originate live

broadcasts. Communities serviced are those unable due to topography to receive any adequate signal from a Canadian radio station and yet not large enough to support their own local station.
That is exactly the situation in the parts of my constituency that I have mentioned and I think the size of the population fully justifies the installation of these stations. I have made inquiries about this and I am not altogether convinced that the reason is the reluctance of the C.B.C. to establish these stations.
I would direct the attention of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and the house to the fact that already there are either telephone or telegraph wire services to these communities. From the information which I have gathered from various sources I am rather under the impression that the Canadian Pacific does not want to have to prop up its old poles in order to carry the two more wires that would be required to provide this service.
I do not think that the reluctance of any company, whether telephone or telegraph, to spend money to improve its lines should prevent communities having radio reception. These communities are producing considerable wealth. For example, last year over a million dollars worth of lumber products were shipped out of Nakusp, and other communities are producing minerals in a similar ratio. I bring this to the attention of the house at the request of the people of my constituency and of a number of organizations who direct my attention to the fact that they will not be able to hear the Easter programs sent out by Canadian stations.
These Canadians in Kootenay West are unable to enjoy Canadian programs while a great majority of Canadians are able to enjoy television. In fairness to these people I contend that serious consideration should be given regardless of the difficulties. The expense is not too great especially in relation to the expensive services which are rendered to other Canadians. Low power relay transmitters should be installed at the two or three points necessary so that these good people may be able to enjoy the C.B.C. and Canadian programs rather than to be forced to listen day after day, week after week, month after month and year after year to United States programs and newscasts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the grievance to which I should like to refer this afternoon arises out of an announcement made the day before yesterday that 1,000 workers would be laid off at the Orenda engine plant. This would be in addition to the 2,000 which it was announced would be laid off by A. V. Roe company.
6, 1855
A. V. Roe Company-Lay-offs This will affect the unemployment situation considerably. The announcement has been made that certain steps will be taken to reallocate these people in other industries. I suggest that this recent announcement will have a most serious effect on the whole Canadian aircraft situation and it is for that reason that I bring it to the attention of the house.
We have in the Canadian aircraft industry the finest designers in the world who have been capable of designing civilian aircraft capable of competing with any aircraft in the world. As the result of government direction, civilian production of these designs has to be set aside to provide for the production of military aircraft. As a result of recent government orders cutting back military production we have had the laying off of aircraft workers who are skilled in their trade. These workers will be lost to the industry, their earnings and standard of living will be reduced.
The encouragement by the government for the design of civilian aircraft has been absolutely nil and the result of this policy will be that there will be nothing to replace the man hours lost in these aeroplane plants because of the reduction in military orders. I suggest that either a policy should be adopted of continuing production at the present level in order to keep these aircraft workers busy until the designers can get their civilian production going, or the announcement should be made by the government that they will not interfere with civilian production. The industry could then run a civilian production line parallel with the military production line.
We have had three separate lay-offs of 1,000 each directly due to government interference, and we do not know what the end will be. Each time we have had some assurance that there Will be no further lay-offs. I consider this a serious grievance to lay before the house and I submit there should be some definite announcement as to when there will be an end to this piecemeal separation of the aircraft industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it was with considerable regret that yesterday the right hon. Prime Minister informed us that Sir Winston Churchill had resigned his portfolio as Prime Minister of Great Britain. I do not think any of us here would for a moment disagree that Mr. Churchill is deserving of his rest and retirement. He has been recognized not only as probably the greatest leader Great Britain has ever had-and some would even go as far as to say that the world has had-but certainly he has been the greatest leader the commonwealth has had.
Because Mr. Churchill has always taken such a great interest in what is now the commonwealth of nations I would like for the next few moments to direct my remarks to this association of nations. If not in years at least in sequence of events it has been a long time since the Pax Britannica of the last half of the last century stabilized the world. As all of us know only too well, the events of the first 50 years of this century have so changed the political aspects of our planet that such a picture would have been completely unforeseeable at the turn of the century. Great powers have risen and fallen; new waves of violent nationalisms have sprung up and are running their course, and the struggle for men's minds is presently continuing between two great political and economic ideologies.
The great British Empire, which has contributed so much to mankind in the science of government, law, fields of literature, the natural sciences and in human standards of decency and morality, has survived two great world wars and has been a victor in both. But what was once the British Empire has now so altered its original form, and is continuing to do so to such an extent, that it has become almost unrecognizable when compared with what it was when Sir Winston Churchill started his political career 50 years ago.
As all of us know, in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the industrial revolution in Great Britain, together with her resources of iron and coal-and what is more important, the stability, perseverance and determination of her people-made Britain by far the most powerful country in the world and extended her territorial possessions, culture, language and government to every corner of the globe. Beginning in the last century, and almost completed in this century, a peaceful evolution has taken place and is continuing to run its course in the various territorial parts of what once constituted this great empire which was originally ruled from England. Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India,

External Affairs
Pakistan and Ceylon have all become, largely in an orderly and peaceful manner, completely independent countries. Other sections such as Burma and the southern part of Ireland have not only become independent but have withdrawn from even a nominal association with the other countries that now form what we know as the British commonwealth of nations.
It is toward this arrangement known as the commonwealth of nations that I should like to direct my remarks for the next few moments. The commonwealth is a type of political arrangement that was previously unknown in recorded history, although in its earlier stages the Delian confederacy of classic Greece was in some ways similar. These independent countries forming the present commonwealth all have various and diverse nationalistic aims which frequently cause members of the commonwealth to come at least into diplomatic conflict with each other. For instance, India and Pakistan have certainly had some diplomatic conflict with each other over Kashmir. India and South Africa are not exactly upon the friendliest terms with each other. Also, these various independent units of the commonwealth compete with each other economically as, for instance, Canada and New Zealand with respect to the export of cheese. Yet despite all this, all these countries, whether they be kingdoms or republics, recognize Her Majesty as the titular head of the commonwealth.
People in other lands outside of the commonwealth find this paradoxical arrangement very difficult to understand. They ask, in the light of present conditions, what is the commonwealth? The units are independent and there is certainly no unanimity as far as foreign policy is concerned. They say "You struggle against each other for world markets, yet you call yourselves members of a family of nations with a queen as its head, although you are racially and culturally totally different groups".
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that as things stand at the moment, and as far as the present trend of the commonwealth is concerned, I find myself among this group of inquiring people wondering what the commonwealth really is at the present time. We all know that at the present time various members of the commonwealth act as liaison officers and interpreters between the two great power blocs of the world, namely the United States on the one hand and the Russo-Chinese bloc on the other. We know that Canada often is called upon to interpret and possibly even mediate difficulties and differences of opinion between the United States

and England, and we have heard that India has a somewhat more direct pipe line to Peking than have some other members of the commonwealth. In that respect the liaison is created between communist China and the western world, a liaison that of course is becoming increasingly important at the present time.
We know that in most cases there is more than the usual friendly association between the governments of the commonwealth countries; we know that occasionally conferences are held to discuss undisclosed problems, whatever they may be. But what else is there to this association which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and others have described as a friendly and easy-going association?
I should like to ask what is the basic difference between our association with commonwealth countries and say the republic of France or Brazil? Do we not have a friendly and easy-going association with these countries? What is the basic difference between the commonwealth and the United Nations? That is the question I have been wondering about, and I think a great many of us have been wondering about. I hope the Prime Minister or more probably the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he sums up the debate on this resolution will enlighten us a little further.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that if at all possible something should be done toward strengthening the relationship between various units of the commonwealth. There is no doubt that the present trend of commonwealth countries is to become less and less associated with each other, and the inevitable result will be the complete dissolution of the commonwealth.
This trend has become most marked and greatly accelerated since the end of world war II. As we all know, new power blocs and new nationalisms have sprung up around the world since then. Canada and England are members of NATO, whereas India, Australia and Pakistan are not. Australia and New Zealand are members of ANZUS and Canada is not. India apparently has aspirations to remain completely neutral and become the leader of the new nationalism in Asia. Pakistan seems to be more favourably inclined toward the west. We have all seen in the past that the break-up of great empires leaves a power vacuum, and in this world of ours some other power group will inevitably move into such a vacuum.
We do not have to go back very far in history to see this. The Austro-Hungarian empire, which had kept middle Europe unified for centuries and which acted as an effective block to the territorial ambitions

of other states for many years, was dismembered after world war I. This was a well-meant dismemberment, I do not doubt, and brings to mind Woodrow Wilson and his doctrine of self-determination of nations, a very commendable doctrine which has resulted in something that I am afraid Mr. Woodrow Wilson did not foresee. We all know that the only result of this dismemberment was a group of weak states in central Europe forming alliances with different power blocs, and in the end they were independently too weak to resist German aggression under the late unlamented Adolf Hitler.
For many years prior to world war II the press and others in the United States continually advocated the break-up of the British Empire, and accused England of repressing subject peoples. This attitude was even reflected by the late President Roosevelt on different occasions during world war II. Well, since world war II this group have had their wish. It would seem to me that these same persons are now perhaps wishing they had not been so anxious to see the British Empire dismembered, because this resulting power vacuum has already been created in places like Burma and India, with consequent alarm to the United States in its new role of world leader.
Oddly enough, Mr. Speaker, in India, Pakistan and elsewhere I understand from personal knowledge at the present time this group of Americans who so earnestly advocated freedom for these countries are by no means popular, and in India and Pakistan the British people are by no means unpopular. It is a rather strange result, but I suppose it points the moral that sometimes we should keep our noses out of other people's business.
However, to continue, if this same situation should ultimately result in a different way with the other nations of the commonwealth the whole course of history will undoubtedly be changed, and I am afraid not for the better. It is quite true that we have the United Nations, and that if open aggression were to take place against a country such as India the United Nations would come to India's aid, as some members of the United Nations did in the case of South Korea. However, in the world of today there are various ways of committing aggression, as we all know. For example country A, let us call it, may instigate and be completely responsible for aggression, yet sit blandly back and be like Caesar's wife, above reproach.
What I meant by this is that it is possible for country A, by promoting internal revolution and similar methods in country B, to 50433-182J
External Affairs
be responsible for setting up a government in country B that will acquiesce and make that country a satellite of country A. One of the most recent examples I can think of is the situation that developed between Russia and Czechoslovakia, and it is not inconceivable that a similar situation could happen in India, Indonesia or Burma at the present time, or in many other places. Undoubtedly the United Nations under such circumstances would find it theoretically very difficult to interfere in what would apparently be the internal affairs of a member nation.
This is just an example to show that it is not always wise to rely entirely upon the United Nations. I think it further shows that countries should develop their own defence forces or join in mutual aid pacts, as has been well illustrated throughout the world in cases such as NATO, ANZUS, SEATO to a lesser extent, and so forth. I think it might be wise-and I shall deal with this in a moment or two-if some consideration were given to forming some sort of commonwealth defence pact, not so much as a bulwark against world war III, although I think it would help in that respect, as against limited aggression on the periphery of the Soviet-controlled empire.
The type of war and aggression we have had almost constantly since 1945 has not been major war but limited aggression here and there using conventional weapons. All of us fear the possibility of a major holocaust with hydrogen bombs. But because of the very danger of such bombs, as has been pointed out to the house many times, we may never get that; but we may have constant pressure and piecemeal wars using conventional weapons and a constant whittling away at territories on the edge of the communist world. Some of the members of the commonwealth are not able to defend themselves, but by the formation of a pact with the other members of the commonwealth I think this type of aggression could be effectively resisted.
I fully realize that the problems would be very great in attempting to arrest the present trend among commonwealth countries. As I have already mentioned, the units of the commonwealth have different political aspirations, and often opposing economic aims and different cultural and racial backgrounds. However, I do feel that if some member of the commonwealth took the lead in this matter a much stronger relationship could somehow be worked out among the commonwealth countries. I think this strengthening of the bonds among the commonwealth countries is necessary as an added assurance for world peace and the ultimate prevention of world war III.

External Affairs
At present the two great armed giants of the world, the United States and Russia, sit scowling at each other on opposite sides of the world. There is no other country or group of countries at the present time that could even hope to challenge the might of either of these countries. If, however, the relationship between the commonwealth countries were strengthened it might conceivably lead to a third power bloc which would be powerful enough to act as a counterbalance to the United States and Russia. This, of course, is probably only a fond hope, but I do not think there is any harm in trying. I am not suggesting for one moment that at the present time the commonwealth countries should act with one voice in the matter of foreign affairs, because that is a practical impossibility; but I do feel that if steps were taken to strengthen the commonwealth relationship this one voice in foreign affairs might not, some time in the future, be as practically impossible as it is now.
I understand that efforts have been made by at least one member of the commonwealth to set up an intercommonwealth defence force, but that these efforts came to naught since the suggestion received a lukewarm reception on the part of two of the members of the commonwealth who participated in the talks, and I understand that Canada was one of them. However, it may be that the effort made was not strong enough or that the ground for the proposal was not properly prepared. As I mentioned earlier, we all know the great value of the commonwealth in acting as interpreter between the American and Russian blocs, but surely it could be something more than just that.
I should like to see Canada take the lead and openly make a determined effort to greatly strengthen the political bonds between the various units of the commonwealth. I suggest Canada because if England were to try to do it undoubtedly it would make countries that are newly independent, such as India, Pakistan and Ceylon, suspicious; but I do not think these countries would be suspicious of Canada or of our motives or intentions. Everyone knows we have no desire for territorial gain or any wish to dominate any other country either directly or indirectly.
Our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), as a result of his past work in the United Nations, is widely respected throughout the entire world, and I might say, properly so. I feel that he might be the man, if the government felt so inclined, to do the job of strengthening the commonwealth and arresting the present trend toward dissolution. A strengthened commonwealth which would make it quite clear to the world that in a great emergency it would act as a unit to

resist aggression could certainly be a decisive factor in preserving world peace. As I mentioned before, I think this is necessary because in the light of the events of the past few years I do not think the United Nations could be relied upon entirely to prevent armed aggression either openly or indirectly by subversion and internal revolution.
It is only a suggestion, but I feel the first step that might be taken toward closer commonwealth association would be to set up a central secretariat, possibly located in Canada or even in some other country if necessary. I know full well there is a close relationship between commonwealth countries through the high commissioners' offices.
I am quite aware of that, but the psychological effect of having a central secretariat for the commonwealth would be very great, and from then on I am sure other steps might well follow toward closer association.
Another suggestion would be that the prime ministers of the various commonwealth units might have meetings, more often if necessary but at least annual meetings. These would be just preliminary steps along the road in the opposite direction to which the commonwealth is going at the moment. As I mentioned earlier, I think if an effort were made by this country, with the ground properly prepared, there might be a stronger possibility of having some intercommonwealth defence force, which might well be the answer for reasons I have already pointed out and shall not repeat. Such a step is probably impractical at the moment, but I feel it could be worked out.
Nationalism can sometimes be a strong force for good but misguided nationalism- and we see evidence of it in nearly every commonwealth country, even here-is just the opposite. If each member of the commonwealth continues to be determined to be its own little empire builder and is not prepared to give up, in some small respect, any of its national sovereignty we shall, as the old expression goes, "all hang separately since we won't hang together." However, if we bind ourselves closer together the commonwealth family may yet be the deciding factor in saving the world from annihilation.
All through the world we hear the argument that every country must give up some of its national sovereignty for the purpose of some form of world government or international control, and I think the commonwealth, because of our past associations, would be a good place to start and set an example to others. I think it can be done if someone makes a determined effort and gives strong leadership; and again, and finally, I think Canada is the nation to do it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I rise to support as strongly as I can, Mr. Speaker, the position taken by my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he spoke in this debate on March 24. As the minister and members of the house will recall, my leader made it crystal clear on that occasion, as he has on other occasions, that we feel the people of Canada do not want to get involved in United States policy with respect to Formosa, Quemoy, Matsu and other areas in the Far East. He made it clear also that we feel Canadian foreign policy should be made here in Ottawa, not in Washington.
In that position, Mr. Speaker, we find ourselves in agreement with statements that have been made on earlier occasions by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). In fact until fairly recently, perhaps until his recent speech before the Canadian Club in Toronto, we were satisfied with the position taken by the minister in that he said many times that Canada has no commitments in that part of the world other than any commitments that might arise because of our membership in the United Nations.
However, we feel from the statement made by the minister in his Toronto speech and from the explanation of that statement which he made in this house on March 24, that that position has been qualified. It seems to us that the position of the government now is that Canada does not agree with the attitude Mr. Dulles takes towards the possible defence of Quemoy or Matsu. It is the policy of the Canadian government that we do not intend to get involved in any war over the defence of these islands. Indeed, we are not committed to take part in any war with respect to the defence of Formosa. However, the minister goes on and suggests that what might start out as a small war could become a big war and if the United States found itself in a big war, no matter how it started, Canada would find itself involved.
Now, if the minister were merely saying that if a world-wide conflagration breaks out, particularly bearing in mind the power blocs that exist in the world today, because of our geographical position, to put it in the vernacular, we would have had it, one could hardly argue with him. But it seems to us that the kind of statement he has made-I refer to his statement in Toronto before the Canadian Club and his explanation of that statement in this house-weakens his position with regard to any further representations he might make to Washington.
We feel the result is that Canada has said that we regard ourselves as quite free to
External Affairs
make any decisions we want with regard to foreign policy, so long as they are agreed to by Washington. In our view the minister should take another look at the statements he has made and try to repair the damage that we feel was done. He should try to make it clear again to the United States that Canada does not believe it is a good idea to get involved in a war over Quemoy or Matsu; indeed, that we should not be a party to United States attempts to keep the Chinese civil war going.
If there is a difference between the approach of the United States to the situation in the Far East and the approach of the United Kingdom, I think it was well put in an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen last night. I have not the editorial before me, but as I recall its content it went something like this. The United States seems anxious to keep that civil war going in the hope that it may eventually result in Chiang Kai-shek getting control of the mainland again. On the other hand, the United Kingdom feels that it is time that civil war was liquidated and brought to a conclusion.
No one in this house can say of the former prime minister of the United Kingdom, Sir Winston Churchill, or of the new Prime Minister, Sir Anthony Eden, that either of these gentlemen is an appeaser, that either of these gentlemen would follow a policy of weakness. Yet we all know that it was the policy of Sir Winston Churchill's government, and we have every reason to believe it is the policy of Sir Anthony Eden's government, that the United Kingdom should not do anything to keep the Chinese civil war going.
We feel that our interests in this matter, despite our geographical proximity to the United States, are closer to the interests of the United Kingdom than they are to the interests of the United States. As I see it, United States foreign policy, particularly under the direction of Mr. Dulles, is built not so much on a diplomatic basis, not so much on a basis designed to avoid war itself, as it is in terms of military strategy. The United Kingdom on the other hand realizes that if a world war breaks out, those islands have had it.
I suggest we are in the same position. Geographically we are close to the United States; but if there should be a conflict between the two great powers in the world today it is now a trite statement to say that we are in the position of a Belgium, and we have had it.
In that sense I feel that our interests are very close to those of the United Kingdom. Both of us have a tremendous stake in avoiding the outbreak of war of any kind because

External Affairs
our two countries know that if that happens there will be devastation of our lands. For that reason, apart from the other connections we have with the United Kingdom, I feel that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should be ranging himself and his policy with respect to the Far East more along the lines advocated by the government of the United Kingdom than along the lines advocated by the government of the United States as set out by Mr. Dulles.
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs should take another look at Mr. Dulles' foreign policy. It is clear. He has spelled it out time and again. It is there for all to read. In my opinion it is not correct to call it a foreign policy; it is a military policy. When he speaks one feels he is not a diplomat who is trying to save the peace of the world, but rather a military strategist planning his moves on the assumption there is going to be an armed conflict in which the United States will be involved.
Mr. Dulles likes to draw that line we have heard him draw, starting from the Aleutians. I am going to describe the line he draws, but for obvious reasons I shall start at the other end. He draws a line from New Zealand up through Australia, the Philippines, Formosa, the Pescadores, Japan, Korea and the Aleutian islands. Does he stop there? No; in his mind that line goes on through northern Canada.
What is that line? Is it a line he has drawn because he is interested in the people on the Pescadores or the people in New Zealand or the people in Churchill, Manitoba? No; it is a defence line for continental United States. In other words all these countries through which that line is drawn by Mr. Dulles are pawns in American military defence strategy.
We should recognize that is what it is, and try to say to Mr. Dulles that we do not appreciate and do not approve of that kind of policy, because our interests appear to be different from the interests of people in the United States, under their present leadership. They seem to have the idea that there can be a war, and that if they have a line of defence around the world other people may perish and other lands may be devastated -whether it be Formosa, northern Manitoba or New Zealand-but that somehow or other the United States will remain intact.
I am sure we in Canada do not look at it in that way, any more than do the people of the United Kingdom. The people of the United Kingdom know that their only defence is in the maintenance of peace, and I suggest that we in Canada know the same thing. We realize that, despite this grandiose

Maginot line that Mr. Dulles would draw from New Zealand right around to Newfoundland, if war broke out there would be devastation and suffering in all the countries through which that line goes.
So I say that this policy on the part of Mr. Dulles is there for all to see and to observe. He spells it out clearly enough. But I repeat that, as I see it, it is not a diplomatic policy. It is not a position arrived at by a foreign minister. It is a position arrived at by a minister of war. It is a matter of military strategy. And I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that, as I have known him across the years, I do not believe he thinks in those terms at all. He thinks rather of his job in terms of the maintenance of peace. He thinks of his job as concerned with getting at the causes of war. He has made many speeches along that line which I would have been very proud to have made myself, and I am satisfied that is his approach-the approach of a foreign minister rather than that of a minister of defence or a minister of war.
I strongly appeal to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as did my leader on March 24, to take another look at this United States policy in which we are involved as just another pawn along with the Pescadores, along with Korea, along with the Aleutians, along with New Zealand and Australia, for the defence of continental United States, on what I say is a false premise, the notion that if you have a strong enough Maginot line some people somewhere can be protected.
Our interests, I repeat, are like those of the United Kingdom. We know, with them, that our only real defence is in the avoidance of war; and we in this group feel that we are expressing the views of many Canadians when we say we do not think the present policy of Mr. Dulles contributes to the avoidance of war as much as would policies which I am satisfied our Secretary of State for External Affairs could advocate, if he would stand up a little straighter on his own two feet and express his own views, as Canadian views, rather than always defending the views put forward by Mr. Dulles.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon, member a question? Does he not feel that it is the purpose of Mr. Dulles in his policy, whatever my hon. friend may call it, to avoid war?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think it is Mr. Dulles' primary purpose to keep war away from the United States, but I am not convinced that Mr. Dulles is as concerned with avoiding war completely as I believe the minister is. If he can keep war away from the United States-if he can keep it in the Pescadores,

in Quemoy, in Matsu or in northern Canada -his aim is met. His aim is to keep war away from continental United States.
I think my hon. friend across the way would like to see the whole world spared the holocaust and tragedy of another war. I am sorry that my hon. friend, even while I am asking him to stand on his own two feet and talk plainly to Mr. Dulles, chooses rather to stand up and defend him. Mr. Dulles does not feel the need of any defence so far as his position is concerned. He stands up and speaks out very clearly and very plainly, and I think our foreign minister should do the same thing, and advocate more clearly a strong Canadian policy.
In connection with this whole business of the defence line, the line for the defence of the United States which Mr. Dulles draws, I have said that while I have heard him draw it, starting from the Aleutians and going around and down to New Zealand, we all know that in his mind it goes across northern Canada; certainly through the distant early warning line, as well as perhaps through the McGill fence and also through "Pinetree". But this does raise some interesting questions. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that we are not necessarily committed to any war the United States may get into, but that we could not help getting involved in the consequences. I think some attention might be paid to the question that was-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: He did not say we would be; he said we might be.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I never said we could not help being involved, in any context in which my hon. friend has used the expression.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The minister said where the United States was involved-and if there is any difference I would be glad to have it corrected-we might-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is an important difference.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not wish to do my hon. friend any injustice. I would tell him that I think he has it in him to enunciate the kind of policy that would ease world tension if he would stand up and express his own views, instead of feeling that he has to go along so easily and so readily with the views of the United States secretary of state.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE

speechtext:
I think at some point the minister should deal with the question to which I started to refer, and that was discussed a while ago in Saturday Night, as to what Canada's position would be with respect to United States troops-air force or others- in this country, if the United States should
External Affairs
get into one of these smaller wars that we would not regard as a Canadian war. As he knows, it is pretty generally remembered that one of the reasons Mr. King did not want to go ahead in 1938 with the British commonwealth air training plan was this very point as to what would happen if we had British troops in Canada at a time when Great Britain became involved in a war into which Canada had not gone. Would we have to intern those troops in order to assert our neutrality, or would failure to do that automatically place us in the position that we were at war?
That is a question which can arise under the present situation, particularly in view of the minister's statement that if the United States got into a small war over Quemoy or Matsu we would not be in it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend apply that argument to our troops in Europe?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am asking the question, and I think it should be dealt with by the minister. He should deal with the question asked by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) as well as the question I have asked. Surely our primary concern is as to our position regarding troops of another nation in our country, particularly in view of the minister's uncertain statement. I think I am justified in using that word describing what our position would be if the United States gets into a war.
We in this house are proud of our Canadian sovereignty. If I may refer to the remarks of the last speaker, we are proud of our position within the commonwealth of nations. We are proud of that association, but we are proud of the fact that within that association we have sovereignty and autonomy. One of the things which took a long while to develop was our own voice as distinguished from that of Westminster in foreign affairs. It is a matter of regret to some of us that the parroting of the foreign policy of the United Kingdom seems to have been exchanged for the same thing with respect to Washington. There is a touch of irony about it in that we seem to have reached this state of affairs at a time when by a process of juxtaposition we now find our interests much closer to those of the United Kingdom in world politics and in foreign policy than used to be the case.
I do not advocate that we should go back to the former position of having our foreign policy written for us at Westminster, but I suggest that the views being held over there at the present time have an element of wisdom in them which is lacking in some of the views being advocated in the country to the south.

External Affairs
There are just one or two other things I want to say in support of the position taken by my leader when he spoke on March 24. We should be giving serious thought, in so far as we have any influence at all, to the continuing policy of the United States in making these atomic and hydrogen bomb tests. We have been able to get a little information out of the government by questions on the orders of the day or on the order paper, but it is precious little. Some of us feel that there is a conspiracy of silence, an unwillingness to tell the people all that is known by scientists and those in the ranks of government with regard to radioactive precipitation. There seems to be such a tendency to rely on atomic and nuclear weapons as a means of defence that we do not know whether as part of our desire to build up that defence we are doing irreparable damage to future generations.
It seems to me that the Canadian people should be treated as grown-ups and that this conspiracy of silence should be broken. We should be told whether any knowledge is available on the matter, and if knowledge is available we should be told what the level of radioactivity is and whether it is doing any present or permanent damage to human life upon this earth.

speechtext: In fairness I think my hon. friend should refer to the statement given on Monday, when there certainly was not a reluctance to give all the information available at this time as far as this country is concerned.

speechtext:
That is the minister's view, but I have had three questions on the subject on the order paper since March 25 and they have not yet been answered. Several of us have asked questions on the orders of the day to which we have not been able to get satisfactory answers. I read with interest the statement the Minister of National Health and Welfare put on Monday's Hansard, but it seems to me that that statement did not answer the fundamental question as to what the level of radioactivity now is as a result of these test explosions, and how far away that level is from the level that could do damage to the human race. Let us not run the risk of doing irreparable damage to future generations, in the name of secrecy, or in the name of defence that might not be defence at all.
I have here a copy of the department's publication External Affairs which deals with the matter, in which it is indicated it is no use our asking the United States to cut down on these tests unless the U.S.S.R. will cut down on them as well. I agree that both
TMr. Knowles.]
these great powers should be asked to withhold these test explosions, but if you cannot persuade the other side are we not being a bit foolish to have both sides running off these explosions if by that result we double the amount of radioactive fall-out with the possibility of going beyond the danger point? This is another one of the fields in which we feel that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should speak strongly on Canada's behalf, if not to the United States authorities at Washington at least within the councils of the United Nations.
I do not want to take up time unduly in this debate, so I shall just refer in passing to two other subjects upon which I had intended to comment. First of all I want to say that I am glad to note that the press of the country for the most part is beginning to accept as being not a bad idea an exchange of parliamentary delegations between the Soviet union and other countries. Statements made in this house on the part of the government so far have been guarded, but at least it does seem to be recognized by some of the newspapers that if such a project were carried through it could not do any harm.
I want to support that idea. Surely an exchange of opinions, surely getting to know what life is like in different parts of the world, cannot do any harm. I do not know whether I can say this without getting a retort of the kind that one gets here in parliament, but I do not think it did me any harm when I had the opportunity of spending a week or so in Moscow back in 1946. I think I learned a few things about the people there. I was interested in the fact that I did have some conversations with people there, some at a semi-official level, and on occasion with people on the street. I do not think it would do others harm to have such a visit, and I am equally sure it would not do any harm from our point of view to invite delegates from that country to come and spend some time freely in our country. It might not do all the good that some might hope, but it certainly would not do any harm. It might help to ease tension if there were a flow of understanding, and I hope we will go ahead with the idea.
The only other comment I wish to make before I resume my seat is something I have commented on before. In fact I feel that I could not partake in a debate on external affairs without saying it. I urge even greater participation by Canada in economic aid and technical assistance programs. Some of the best speeches on this general subject have been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I was sorry that on

March 24 he found it necessary to try to deflate the idea that economic aid could play as important a part in easing tension and building up world peace as some of us think it could. I will be fair to him by admitting that in that speech he said it was important, but he also said-and I quote from page 2338 of Hansard-
-it is easy to lapse into the comfortable belief that we can save Asia

and that is how it is often put-with economic aid alone; that we can buy off communism and purchase peace for ourselves merely by stepping up our economic assistance.
That, as I see it, is unhappily nothing but a comforting illusion; and in saying that I do not minimize the importance of such economic assistance.
Mr. Speaker, none of us would claim that economic assistance, particularly if it is handing out aid on a relief basis, can itself buy off communism or save the peace. But what I do not like about statements such as that is that they seem to be excuses for keeping the program down to the rather low proportions of Canada's participation in this field.
There is a great deal that could be done along the lines that have been set out by the minister on a number of occasions. Much could be done by greater support to organizations like the world health organization. There is much that could be done by greater support of training programs, bringing people from other countries to Canada, training and educating them here so they could go back to help put their own countries on a better economic footing. There is much to be done in teaching these people the ways of democracy and the way of life we have found.
I submit that until we have gone all out, until we have increased many times what we are doing now in terms of economic aid, there is no room for saying this will not do the trick. We have not yet tried it to a worthwhile extent; we have just scratched the surface. In my view there is a tremendous opportunity for the easing of world tensions, for the removal of the causes of war and building the foundations for a better world in a vast program of economic aid. I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who in his heart is, I think, just as sold on this type of program as any of us, will not make these statements in which he detracts from the value of economic aid but will push for an even greater program as part of an over-all aim to save the peace and make for a future that instead of bringing war will hold a better life for all mankind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to disagree strongly with the opinion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre of Mr. Dulles' efforts to keep the United States and the world out of war. I think that Mr. Dulles makes mistakes-we 50433-183
External Affairs
all do-but I believe he is certainly intent on keeping the world out of war just as much as his own United States. I think it is rather unfair to imply that he would sacrifice other countries in a war as long as the United States remained out.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs made very clear the other day that Canada could not remain neutral if the United States became involved in a major war. I feel sure that the great majority of Canadians agree with that statement; and because we are so closely linked to the United States in both peace and war I think we are entitled to point out any actions which we believe are not in the best interests of our mutual safety and well-being.
The latest instance when I think a protest should have been made was at the time of the publication of the Yalta papers. This action, together with the pressure which has been brought to bear by Senator Knowland to publish the Tehran and Potsdam papers, has, I believe, made future high-level secret diplomacy almost impossible. I believe that our chances of avoiding another world war have decreased accordingly. In the past many wars have been avoided because representatives of both sides met in private and, in off the record discussions, ironed out the matters in dispute. This requires give and take on both sides, and it would often have been impossible for either side to give way and come to an agreement if the participants had thought their conversations would be made public in a relatively short space of time.
I believe that in recent years the ineffectiveness of so-called open diplomacy has been demonstrated time and again, both in the security council and in the big four conferences which have been held during the past ten years. It has always been recognized by those engaged in diplomatic work that effective diplomacy can only be carried on in private, and in the knowledge that records of the discussions will not be made public. I feel sure that the professionals of the United States state department recognize this fact; but despite this, those in charge of the political strategy of the Republican party have chosen to greatly reduce the effectiveness of any future diplomatic discussions between the United States and other powers with whom they may be negotiating.
After the publication of the Yalta papers, and the demands of Senator Knowland that the Tehran and Potsdam papers should be published as well, diplomatic discussions participated in by the United States in the future will be no more effective than other open discussions have been in the past.
I believe the only explanation for this extraordinary action is purely political. It

External Affairs
seems to me that the Republican party is so anxious to try to discredit the Democratic party as communist sympathizers that the secretary of state saw fit to authorize the publication of the Yalta papers. The world is required to pay a very high price for a doubtful political game by the party in power in the world's most powerful nation.
The only explanation I can find for the Canadian government not vigorously protesting against this action is that this government understands so well the practice of saying anything which they think will gain votes for them at election time. For example, for 36 years now they have been promising health insurance before every election, with not the slightest intention of ever implementing that promise. So this action of the Republican party in this instance does not appear to the Canadian government to be anything more than routine political practice.
I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that President Eisenhower will soon make it clear that the Tehran and Potsdam papers will not be published, and that the records of all future secret conferences participated in by the United States will remain secret. I believe that only by doing so can high-level diplomacy return to any degree of effectiveness, and our chances of avoiding another world war remain good.
We have told the United States that we will back her 100 per cent if she becomes involved in a major war, and all we are saying to her now in criticizing this action is, "For heaven's sake don't destroy the best known means of avoiding war." I think if the Canadian government had shown more courage in the past in voicing our objections to United States actions which adversely affected us, and with which we disagreed, we would not find ourselves today treated as poor relations in matters affecting trade between the two countries.
I am referring, of course, to the practice of the United States imposing artificial trade restrictions on Canadian products whenever pressure is brought to bear by United States producers. Because the Canadian government has always meekly submitted to the imposition of any trade restrictions the United States government saw fit to impose, they have imposed restrictions whenever and wherever it suited them to do so, and additional restrictions are being considered today.
The United States has always treated Canada as a happy dumping ground for surplus production, and they have kept their factories open and workers employed when Canadian factories were being closed or going half time, and men were being laid off. This, of course, is not the fault of the United States government. They have simply

taken advantage of our easy-going regulations, which have not made this kind of thing impossible.
I think the time is long overdue, Mr. Speaker, for Canada to speak a lot more forcibly and strongly to our neighbours about things which adversely affect us, and with which we disagree and believe unreasonable. Until we do we can only expect to go on being treated as poor relations in matters of trade and other questions which affect our welfare.
