speechtext:
Like other hon. members who have spoken in this debate I intend to confine myself mainly to the Far Eastern situation. However, I should like to say I was rather disappointed when the minister made his statement that he did not make greater reference to the trouble spots in the Middle East.
It would appear to me that with the Arab nations in an uneasy peace with Israel we are apt to have a major conflagration break out at any time. It is about time the United Nations got down to facts and placed the issue squarely before the opposing sides with respect to the trouble they are having there, telling them it is about time they settled down to a definite peace treaty so we can get away from these various border incidents, brought about mainly by the buffer zones between the two factions.
I think, too, it is about time that we told them that unless the United Nations rehabilitation contributions to the Arab refugees are used for rehabilitation they will be stopped. I believe these payments have gone on long enough for the maintenance of those people in the refugee camps. It is about time they were forced to get out and make their own way somehow. It should be made perfectly clear to them that any further rehabilitation grants for the refugees will be used for rehabilitation only and not for maintenance within the camps.
I am going to agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on one thing only, namely that we should increase our financial assistance to the underdeveloped countries of southeast Asia. Because of the small amount of assistance that is going into those countries we are losing the propaganda battle for the souls and the minds of those people. It is quite easy for a communist to walk in there and preach his theories of equality and have those poor downtrodden people believe them, because they cannot realize that the equality that is being preached is equality of oppression rather than equality of opportunity.
However, they tell us that a person who is underprivileged will always listen to big

promises before he will accept and be influenced by a small measure of assistance. Rather than have this half-hearted help go into the south Asian countries we should do everything in our power to see that the suffering of those poor people is alleviated. We should go as far as we can in this assistance. But here is where I differ with the members of the C.C.F. party. I do not think we should at any time grant assistance at the expense of our own preparedness program, because that is of the utmost importance.
As far as Viet Nam and Indo-China are concerned, I think the Canadian delegation on the truce team there is doing a good job. I should like to offer my congratulations at this time to those people who are there doing the best they can, but they have a tremendous job. There is a lot of subterfuge. The so-called troubles that are cropping up among the people are communist inspired, merely put forward as a means of screening the true activities of the communists in Viet Nam.
I would appreciate very much if the minister would make some sort of statement in his rebuttal about the troubles they are having in Saigon at this time. I should like him to tell us whether or not it is an honest difference of opinion among the Viet Nam peoples themselves, or whether it is more or less communist inspired trouble that is being stirred up there at this time.
Peace in Indo-China was brought about with the proviso that general elections will be held in July of 1956. Consultations are supposed to be held between the respective authorities of the two zones from July 20 of this year onward. I wonder whether, when drafting the proviso-I am not too conversant with the details-it was definitely laid down who those competent authorities were to be. If so, who are they, and are they to be trusted? It would appear from our past experience with the communists in Formosa, Korea and elsewhere, that they are not to be trusted. They are not too willing to give up anything they have or to allow free elections to be held which might mean they would lose some area they already hold. For example, under the Korean set-up there were to be free elections held in Korea in 1947. When 1947 rolled around the North Korean reds refused to allow free elections to be held. We do not have to go back that far, because the same thing holds true in East Germany. I do not know when we are to reach any sort of settlement between the two Germanys and have free elections, because it is quite apparent that the communists are unwilling to relinquish anything they have.
I think, too, that we are going to have to be very careful this same thing does not 50433-183J
External Affairs
happen in Burma, in Thailand and in some of the other countries of southeast Asia. For example, the prime minister of Thailand, when speaking at the SEATO meeting not long ago, stated that there were something like 20,000 so-called free Thailand troops assembled in Yunan province of red China, which could be used for a jumping off place for an invasion against Thailand itself. I understand the Burmese premier also stated that they had the same state of affairs on the northern Burma border. There they have a bunch of Burmese communists waiting for an opportunity to invade northern Burma and possibly divide that country in the same way that Korea and Indo-China have been divided.
There is one other point that has nothing to do with the communist element in southeast Asia, but can the minister indicate whether or not any progress has been made in the withdrawal of the nationalist troops in northern Burma? He will recollect that a year ago last fall a formal protest was lodged with the United Nations by the Burmese government, and it was suggested at that time that the Chinese nationalists should do everything in their power to convince these people that they should go back to Formosa. That was quite a sore spot as far as the Burmese government was concerned, and we have not heard too much about the matter since. I should like the minister to tell us in his rebuttal whether or not there has been any mass withdrawal or whether subsequent withdrawals have only been on a piecemeal basis.

speechtext: As I may not have much, if any, time for rebuttal, perhaps I could answer that question at once by saying that a good proportion of these so-called Chinese troops have been moved back to Formosa from Burma.

speechtext:
I am glad the minister has made that statement, because there is no doubt that was one factor that could possibly turn Burma against the western world in the event of warfare commencing in Asia.
As to the islands of Quemoy and Matsu, I am not sure whether they are too strategic.
I do not have the information, and it is a matter for military opinion. But as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) mentioned the other day, they can have quite a value from the point of view of morale as far as the Chinese nationalists are concerned. Canada has no commitment there consequent upon actual invasion of the islands, but I suggest that they certainly are a matter of great interest to the Asiatic peoples and stand as a symbol of whether or not we are going to retreat any further. There is no doubt

External Affairs
that the Chinese reds are going to take everything they can get. They are going to keep walking ahead just as long as they can do so without hindrance. We must also remember that since the Chinese communists came into power in 1949 they have simply led the world from one crisis to another, in Korea, Indo-China and Tibet. All the time they have been gradually working their way into the other countries of Asia, and it is about time they were stopped.
We have to lay down a certain line and say they are not going to be allowed to go beyond it. We have to make sure they do not go beyond it. Whether or not the islands of Matsu and Quemoy should constitute that line I do not know. That depends entirely on the tactical situation, and that is a matter for the military authorities to decide. As to the Chinese reds having good intentions, in my opinion their intentions are in no way honourable. I do not think their only aim in Asia is to regain Chinese territory, including Formosa and the Pescadores, because in my view they intend to proceed farther and farther into Asia and spread their tentacles as far as they can.
It has been said in the house from time to time that the ultimate aim of the communists is world domination. That applies not only to the Moscow reds but to the Chinese reds as well. Not long ago Mr. Khrushchev, when speaking at a meeting between the Chinese and the Russians, said:
The Chinese people's republic has transformed itself into a powerful factor in the liberation struggle of all oppressed peoples against the forces of imperialist reaction and colonial enslavement for their freedom and national independence. The Chinese people's republic has entered the world arena as a great power and has become a mighty force in the general struggle of the freedom-loving peoples for international security and peace throughout the world.
This means only one thing, that the Chinese reds have joined with their Russian brothers in an effort to spread communism throughout the world and to free all the peoples of the world, whether or not they want to be free. I also doubt-and here is where I differ very strongly with the members of the C.C.F. group-whether or not withdrawal from Matsu, Quemoy or any other place would serve the interests of peace. Rather, I think it would work the other way. If we give up without a struggle here, there and everywhere, it is going to encourage them to take one more little piece of land. It is all too reminiscent of Munich and the peaceful overtures made to Hitler prior to 1939 when he took everything he could get and kept on going until he forced us into war.
I think the only possibility is to serve notice on the Chinese reds now that they

have gone as far as they can go, and we should threaten them with retaliation if they go any farther. I do not think that would be anything to start a world war. Peace and security cannot be promoted by indefinitely piling up one-sided concessions to the reds. For example, may I refer to the radio comment from Peking on the withdrawal from the Tachen islands. They said:
The liberation of these islands has created favourable conditions for our people's liberation army in the liberation of Formosa.
That is plain enough. They are going ahead unless we put our foot down. I forget the exact words the Secretary of State for External Affairs used, but when he was making his statement the other day he said that it was significant there was no resistance to the withdrawal from the Tachen islands. I do not think there is anything significant in that because nobody is going to fight for something they are going to get anyway. In my opinion that withdrawal did more to hurt the prestige of the western nations in the east than anything else could have done.
I think one outcome of our withdrawal from time to time is the present attitude of the Chinese reds. They are actually contemptuous now. When they were asked in 1951 to join in a conference respecting Korea they accepted, but when they were recently asked to confer with the security council of the United Nations they simply said they would not unless they could come there on their own terms, which meant removing the Chinese nationalists from the United Nations and giving the Chinese communists their seat. That indicates they are becoming more and more contemptuous and more and more sure of themselves as our withdrawals become more general. I believe another result of all these withdrawals is that the non-communist peoples are beginning to become a bit more afraid that maybe we are not going to back up our statements of policy and our threats against the communists. The free nations, particularly the United States, did a lot of big talking about what they were going to do before the fall of Dien Bien Phu, and it certainly did not help our prestige in southeast Asia one bit.
As I said a few moments ago, we also aided in the evacuation of the Tachen islands, and that did not do any good. I think any further withdrawal by the western nations could quite easily be interpreted as a sign of weakness by the southeast Asian countries, and it would certainly weaken our bargaining powers as far as any cease-fire is concerned.
The reason I believe a stand now would not cause any world war is that I do not think the communists are ready for it yet. I do not

think 'Russia is going to allow the Chinese to throw her into a war at this time because she is not in any position to back up China to the extent she would like, so far as arms and munitions are concerned.
The Soviet goals, as we all know, are to advance the Soviet sphere of influence so far as they can into Europe, Asia, the Middle East and so on, and at the same time retain the predominant position which they attained in 1950 in eastern Europe, Mongolia and North Korea. I think Russia realizes that so far as Mongolia and Korea are concerned she has lost a lot of ground, because the Chinese reds have taken a lot away from her. Russia feels also that she has to protect her own people within the Soviet union, at least to an extent which would stop them from engaging in out and out revolution. Russia is not going to go beyond that point in assisting the Chinese reds.
Communist China, of course, has the ultimate aim of spreading not only the communist influence but the Chinese communist influence all through Asia. It is significant to note that the Asiatic communists are turning now to Mao and his government rather than to the Kremlin. As a result, I think by holding these people back at the moment, eventually their disagreements are going to become so great that they are going to have a little scrap among themselves. As long as everything is going their way and they are walking ahead without any trouble at all there certainly is not any hope of breaking up that agreement and friendship which they now have. We have to stand firm. I think the differences in aims between the two peoples, and the places where they conflict, are going to do a great deal toward breaking down the communist influence throughout the world. I do not think they can get along among themselves.
I have just one more point, Mr. Speaker. This debate has been very interesting, in that at least it has shown the difference in viewpoints between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the C.C.F. party. (socialist) party, conti lued to pursue his vigorously left of Liberal policy. But when Woodsworth came out
External Affairs

Woodsworth was admired in Ottawa for his biting wit, sharp writing and occasional Donald Duck editorial rages. His portside politics evidently never troubled Canada's ruling Liberals. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate I would open my remarks by making a very brief reference to the hon. member for Wetas-kiwin (Mr. Thomas), who has just taken his seat. He has taken us through a remarkable tour de force. In a matter of 30 minutes he has expressed his views on Germany, Israel, Egypt, Mongolia, Indo-China, Korea, Quemoy, the Matsus, and communism, and made reference to other political parties. Is that not something? Is it not extraordinary when any man can execute such a tour de force in a period of 30 minutes, when speaking in a debate on external affairs?
It is not my intention to follow the example of the hon. member. As a matter of fact I am not going to speak on any of the phases of external affairs mentioned by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, nor do I intend to mention communism, nor do I intend to imply anything about any political parties in the House of Commons. There is only one phase of external affairs about which I wish to express my opinion, and that is the position and policy of Canada in this age of thermonuclear accomplishments and developments, a matter which is of major concern to all of us irrespective of party, and irrespective of whether we support the government or the opposition.
I feel very deeply on the matter. I have no hesitation in saying that perhaps the limitations of my vocabulary and eloquence will not permit me to express the thoughts that arise in me. To the best of my ability, however, I am going to put them forward and,

unusual as it may be for me, I shall quote at some length from certain references I have before me.
I have said that I am going to discuss only one issue, and that I shall discuss it on a strictly non-political basis. All will agree that Canada is a wonderful country, a country with a population in the neighbourhood of 15 million, and that with this comparatively small population it is one of the outstanding countries of the world. If I remember correctly we are the third trading nation. In his budget speech last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said that other countries look with envy at our fiscal policy. I believe I am safe in saying that at times of world conflict, on a per capita basis this country ranks very close to the top in matters of contributions of manpower and financial assistance. I believe I am also safe in saying that in respect of all various aspects of the work of the United Nations, next to the great powers-the United States, Great Britain and the U.S.S.R.-Canada stands at the top in its work on the committees.
What I am building up to is this. We can all take pride in our country and its accomplishments. Because of our status and our influence among the nations, although a nation of only 15 million people, can we not give consideration now to providing a lead in matters of policy and program in this trying age and these troubled times resulting from the development of thermonuclear weapons? In other words can we not be more emphatic and serve as a leader rather than a follower in international affairs? I am not for one moment attempting to detract from the stand Canada has taken, or from the statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; but I do believe we can go further and do more. I believe Canada can make an outstanding contribution if we are firmer, more deliberate and more emphatic, and if we give a lead.
There can be no question but that we live in trying times. I would not like to have the job held by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; I would not want it for any money. It must be a terrible responsibility. I am sorry the house has not had a full report as to what went on at the recent commonwealth conference. Indeed we are almost in the dark as to the discussions and the conclusions. I have never set myself up as a prophet, but if I were to do a little guessing, and if the procedure followed at the last conference was that followed at previous ones, I would be reasonably sure that on the final day, at the conclusion of the meetings, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent), in his position of priority,

would have made a concluding address. And, sir, if we could be told what he said, I believe it would go like this:
We have met at a time when events from week to week, sometimes from day to day have brought vividly home to us the tension of the European situation, the difficulties that beset those who are striving to bring stability out of unrest and confidence out of fear. Fortunately also we have seen how patient and unremitting are the efforts to repair the torn fabric of European unity, how widespread is the desire and the determination to ensure peace, how deep the reluctance to incur the incalculable hazards of war.
At this time of grave international unrest and anxiety we have sought throughout to avoid, in phrase or gesture, anything which might add to existing difficulties.
Indeed, we have reason to hope that the principles which we have reaffirmed, and the views to which we have given expression, may contribute not a little to a better understanding among all nations, and to a more fruitful collaboration between them.
I do not think I would be far wrong if I said that might indicate what was said by the Prime Minister of Canada and the other prime ministers at the recent commonwealth conference. I would agree with those expressions. But what I have said, as being possibly what was said by our own Prime Minister at the commonwealth conference, is actually what was said by the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King at the conclusion of the imperial conference in 1937. Two years later we were faced with the holocaust of another world war.
Since that time science has developed the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the cobalt bomb and other thermonuclear weapons. I understand that the reactor which Canada has at Chalk River is the second largest in the world, and it is devoted to the development of nuclear fission for peace purposes. Are we therefore not in position to go further than we have gone in the past, in view of the fact that today on the floor of this House of Commons, in the parliaments of the world we hear from the political leaders of the world expressions exactly the same as were made back in 1937. We should realize that someone has to give leadership so we would deal not with generalities and platitudes but with definite policies and programs.
I do a great deal of reading, and I think the wishful thinking and the actual desire and belief of leaders in the parliaments of the western world, truthful as they are, are in line with the expressions which were used just before the second world war. Today we need something more than platitudes and generalities, and I cannot think of a country better able than Canada to take the lead.
We hear and read almost every day statements by scientists as to the probable effects of the detonation of thermonuclear weapons.
External Affairs
There seems to be some doubt as to what might happen. Only recently we were given some assurance by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) as to the genetic results, but do we have to wait until there is human evidence before action is taken?
The position is made clear by the scientists, but no matter what we are told the fact remains that they cannot take action; only parliaments can take action. It is my request that Canada give a lead. First of all Canada should recognize the statements made by the scientists and appreciate the worries of these men who are in a position to know what may happen. Political action should be taken to further investigation and to further a policy which will guarantee that we do not have to face what may happen to human beings or to nature itself because of these explosions of a thermonuclear nature.
I think attention should be paid to what has been said by Dr. O. M. Solandt, chairman of our defence research board. Dr. Solandt made an address to the Canadian Club of Toronto. This was considered to be so important that the information division of the Department of External Affairs saw fit to issue it as a release. Dr. Solandt is one of our great Canadian scientists, and I should like to place on record some of the statements he made because I think they are important and should be heard not only by members of parliament but by the people of Canada. He said:
When the history of this century comes to be written I am sure that it will then be clear that we are living in the midst of one of the greatest periods of transition in human history.
And again:
Nonetheless I think that it is particularly important for us to try to comprehend the significance of the developments in nuclear science that are taking place and try to control and direct their use. Should we fail in this task there seems to be a fair chance that the history of our era will never be written.
And again:
The scientific discoveries that underlie the thermonuclear weapons demonstrated in 1954 open possibilities for the unlimited increase of the destructive power of weapons and consequently face mankind with the ultimate possibility of selfdestruction.
The A.E.C. announcement also emphasized the fact that bombs of this kind produce huge amounts of radioactive fission products which fall out over a vast area which may cover many thousands of square miles.
The reference there is to the United States atomic energy commission. I emphasize that this is a statement by one of our leading scientists. I continue:
Man is therefore faced with a dilemma of a magnitude which he never faced before. The whole

External Affairs
history of civilization is a history of wars. Man has never solved the problem of living without fighting. In the past these wars have wiped out individuals, families, tribes, and even small nations, but the destructive power of the weapons available was never sufficient to destroy the race. We have now reached a stage in' history where we can foresee the possibility of having weapons available in the world in numbers capable of destroying our civilization and of rendering large parts or even the whole of the world uninhabitable by man. This means that our attitude toward war must be fundamentally changed if we are to ensure survival.
The last quotation I want to give is I think perhaps the most important tor this House of Commons.
We must hasten to solve our ancient problems of living together if we are to survive. We are now at last faced with the desperate alternative of one world or none.
That, sir, is an expression of opinion from one of our great Canadian scientists. It is so important that the minister of external affairs had it printed by his department of information. That scientist and others can go no further than to make statements. Action can only be taken by parliament on the recommendation of the government. It is not only the scientists who speak on this theme; it is also spoken of by men in politics. I wish to quote only two such statements made by men of political power. They recognize the danger, but I am afraid they do not follow through or use their political power to back their knowledge. This statement is, I think, important:
Nowhere on this planet today is there an Impregnable fortress, a continent or island so distant that it can ignore all the outer world. If this is not to be the age of atomic hysteria and horror, we must make it the age of international understanding and co-operative peace.
That, sir, was a statement made by the President of the United States before the American newspaper publishers' association in New York on April 22, 1954. In the same speech he also said:
Free men do not lose their patience, their courage, their faith because the obstacles are mountainous, the path uncharted. Given understanding, they invariably rise to the challenge. Never, then, has there been a more compelling and rewarding time to work for international understanding, to labor for a co-operative peace.
That is an expression of opinion by the President of the United States.
I have not hesitated in the past to criticize what I thought were the wrong policies of Mr. Dulles, secretary of state of the United States, because I thought they were wrong, often basically wrong. However, I wish to admit that I do believe he has in mind a vision of what could happen at this time if we had a thermonuclear war. I wish to quote two statements which Mr. Dulles made in a speech delivered before the Y.W.C.A. at their

centennial inaugural luncheon at New York on January 11 of this year. He said:
There will never be permanent peace so long as men and nations reserve for war their greatest effort, their most sacrificial endeavour.
He also said:
But also, peace cannot be won by truculence or by intolerance, either toward our allies or toward our citizenry. Peace has to be planned as a campaign in which many factors are weighed. It is a campaign in which it may be necessary to strive even when success may be improbable.
As I said, I have been critical of some of the policies which I see being followed throughout the world and of policies which have been enunciated by the President of the United States and Mr. Dulles, but I most sincerely agree with the principle expressed in the quotations I have read. I most sincerely believe that we have reached a stage in the development of our civilization and our scientific knowledge when we can no longer rest content with platitudes and generalities. I am convinced that the world is waiting for leadership, and I do believe quite honestly that the status and the influence of Canada is such that if this House of Commons-and that means this government and to a great extent the minister of external affairs-could come forth with a dynamic program and more forthright statements they would receive a great deal more support than is anticipated, and it would be an encouragement not only to the people of the Dominion of Canada but to the free peoples of the world.
I wish to add my remarks to those which have already been expressed on this subject. Not only should this government give more leadership; it should also be prepared not to just accept the position that there are doubts about the efiects in peacetime of the explosion of thermonuclear weapons, but the government should give leadership through its position in NATO in demanding a more comprehensive, thorough and collective study of this problem.
I do not wish to take up much more time of the house. I have tried to express my inner thoughts and to base my address to a great extent on the quotations which I have read. I have made recommendations to the minister of external affairs because I have confidence in the position Canada holds in the world and in the fact that a statement made by the hon. member that is by nature definite, emphatic, dynamic and visionary will be listened to. Let us not forget that it was reported by a Washington correspondent in the newspapers only two days ago that a member of the congress of the United States, one of the best known men in that country, said in discussing the policy concerning

Quemoy and Matsu, that if they came up with a policy that even their greatest ally, Canada, could not accept, what a policy it must be. That indicates the attention that is given to the views of this country and the policies of this government.
In concluding I wish to emphasize the thinking and the principles that are being expressed by the political leaders and scientists of the democratic world, that now is a time of decision, and unless we are careful no history will be written of this day and age because mankind will have ceased to exist on this earth. All, in the expression of their desire for peace, say we must not take a position of antagonism, truculence or suspicion; we must not be held back by obstacles, setbacks and disillusionments, because the future of the world depends upon carrying on our search for peace; because the maintenance of mankind and of civilization depends upon our living together. Otherwise we are going to die together. Yes, we have had and still have suspicions. We have great worries. Without doubt we have had a great many disillusionments and a great many setbacks. But, as even Mr. Dulles said, we have to carry on for a brotherhood of peace.
You know, Mr. Speaker, it has been my privilege to have been a public servant in opposition for some 22 years now. I can assure you that one sometimes reaches a point of frustration. You believe you are right; you know you are right, but you do not seem to be able to make any progress. I have discovered on occasions like that that I can go back to some of the best writers in the world and get the inspiration and the courage to carry on. One of the writers I sometimes go back to- and I commend him to the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he has not read the book to which I am going to refer-is Lloyd C. Douglas and his famous book entitled "Green Light". It is strictly a work of fiction. In that book there is a statement by one of the leading characters, Dean Harcourt, who said in effect: "In my lifetime I, too, have faced obstacles, setbacks, dissillusionments and frustration, but I know that my goal is right; I know that destiny is on my side; I know that eventually I am going to get the green light, and then I am going to go on through."
In all this struggle for peace, Mr. Speaker, in all the trials and tribulations of today, there have been frustrations, I know, to the Secretary of State for External Affairs; there have been setbacks and disillusionment. Very often we are suspicious. May I say, sir, and
External Affairs
I conclude as I started, in this age of thermonuclear discoveries and accomplishments I feel that if the minister, as our spokesman on foreign affairs, will give greater leadership, be more emphatic, more progressive, and will not be set back by disillusionments and frustrations, Canada will give a great lead to the world and eventually we will get the green light that opens the road to a lasting peace.

I have listened with intense interest to the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. If he could only go to Russia and get them to believe just what he has said; if he could only go to China and get them to believe what he said, then probably there would be some sense in what he said because we are all ready to believe it and the people of the free world are ready to believe it, if only the people of the communist world would ease their aggression. But the people of the communist world are determined to continue their aggression until there exists no anti-communist world. I hope the hon. member takes time to think that through before he rises in his place and gives us any more alarming speeches. Our problem is to know what is the calm, sane, sensible thing to do to preserve our freedom in these troubled times.
It is my purpose to give some attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar on March 24. The hon. member made a statement which could be easily interpreted as meaning that the Chinese people drove Chiang Kai-shek from China. That statement, if I have interpreted it correctly, is just as false as a falsehood can be, because Chiang Kai-shek was not driven from China by the Chinese people but by the people of the United States. There is no time remaining for me to establish the position that I have to establish in order to make good that statement, but I shall be right here when this debate resumes.
Let me point out meanwhile that in February, 1945, President Roosevelt, the president of the United States, threw Chiang Kai-shek to the dogs by simply agreeing to allow Russia to have Manchuria, which is the source of most of the industrial strength of China, and north China, which is the source of the rest of the industrial strength of China. To that statement there is positively no answer.
